paragraphs.text: Yesterday my voice was weary, but the grace of God strengthened it through your prayers and your eagerness. Having learned from that experience how much the eager zeal of those who love God can achieve, I come to you with the same appeal: I ask you once more to pray for the same grace on your own behalf. Paul, the chosen vessel, had Christ speaking in him and was guided by the Holy Spirit, yet he secured the prayers of his hearers in advance, saying, "Brothers, pray for me, that words may be given to me when I open my mouth." How much more, then, should we, who are lowly and practically nothing, ask for your intercession. Pray that the bond on my tongue may be loosed and that I may speak boldly. Pray also that divine grace itself may keep the instrument unhindered and supply my thoughts generously. I ask this not so that the one who speaks of divine things may profit alone, but so that he may draw up heavenly riches together with you. Come, then, let us take up where we left off. Moses the lawgiver completed his account of creation in sequence and order. It is fitting, I think, that we too should join the second things to the first and the third to the second, keep a sound judgment, and set out the account for you without confusion. The heaven had been fixed and the firmament set firm. The sea had been marked off and the earth laid bare. The earth had been adorned with fruits, plants, trees and springs, and in short with everything it needed. What sprang up from it was not of one simple kind but diverse and varied. Some things adorned the earth itself. Others became food for human beings or for the animals. Still others were useful to the human beings just mentioned. This is not the time to go through all the different things that sprang up from the earth, for I do not want to weary your ears with a long discourse. The heaven too had received its own adornment. Next God turns to the waters and makes them bring forth living souls. He is the great and all-wise Creator, who made all things by an effortless nod and by his holy word. You learned the truth of these things from the very word of truth when you heard him say, "Let the waters be gathered," and at once the work followed the word. Again he said, "Let the earth bring forth," "Let the waters bring forth," and "Let there be lights." It would take a long time now to go through everything that came into being by a word. Let us leave aside the things of the old creation and come to what he did by a word alone in the New Testament. For he is the one who created the old things and also made the new, according to John, who says, "All things came into being through him, and without him not one thing came into being." What words could explain these things precisely? But let us keep to the sequence. As we said before, this all-wise Creator adorned first what he had made first. To what came into being second he gave its adornment second. In the same way he gave beauty to the third, the fourth and all the rest in turn, according to the order of creation. What was his purpose in this? Perhaps he wanted the very elements to teach us to respect boundaries and recognize order. First, then, he made the heaven above, second the earth, third the firmament, and fourth he separated the waters. What he made first, he adorned first. Some more exacting listener will surely say, "How then did he adorn the earth first, when it came second?" He will want to catch me out, as though my argument contradicted itself. We must answer him that we have said nothing contradictory, and that the argument is entirely consistent. For the earth was adorned before this firmament, which came into being after the heaven above and received its form on the second day. Precedence had to be kept in the sequence. After he had adorned the earth with plants and fruits, and beautified the heaven with the sun, the moon and the rest of the chorus of stars, he came to the waters. And what does the historian say? "And God said," he tells us, "Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds flying above the earth across the firmament of heaven." See how God's word brings works after the words, and how the words accomplish deeds. Look at God's syllables, small words filled with divine power: "Let the waters bring forth." For God, the word is the labor. I think the works ran ahead of the word, for their power was swifter than the utterances. The word had not yet been spoken, and already the work was receiving its proper beauty. And here is the wonderful thing: God gave each of these elements a twofold adornment. To the firmament he gave lights and dew. The uses of these lights also differ, as is clear from the very words of Scripture. We discussed them the other day as well as we could, if not as they deserve, when we set out our account of them, and there is no use in speaking about them again now.

To the earth he gave crops and plants, and to the waters swimming creatures and birds: "Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds flying." He calls the fish "creeping things," since they creep rather than walk. This is why blessed David, following the lawgiver, says, "This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number." It is a strange thing, a strange arrangement, a strange declaration. Why? Because the Maker of all has things past, present and future before his eyes more clearly than we see with our own eyes. He was going to grant life to the world first through the waters, so he lets the waters be the first to bring forth a living nature, so that you may learn where the root of life lies. I see the newly enlightened coming out of the holy waters. They went into baptism with many evils, like creeping things, and they come out with eternal life. When I see this, I see the lawgiver saying, "Let the waters bring forth" those who were once creeping things and are now living souls. How does this become clear to us? Because those who come to the bath of baptism are given the name of creeping things on account of their former sins. Many went out to John's baptism, and he says to those who came, "Serpents, brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" A soul that has lived with wickedness for many years goes into baptism and comes out having put it off. See whether the Master's voice does not shine out through these very deeds, saying, "Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and birds flying." The one who is saved receives a twofold grace. His soul is given life, and from then on he becomes a bird. He reaches the vaults of heaven, lives as a citizen with the angels, and keeps his place in the ranks above. "And birds flying above the earth across the firmament of heaven": above the earth because of the body, in heaven because of the citizenship. We have not brought these things in by allegorizing. We have contemplated them within the history itself. It is one thing to force the history into allegory, and another to keep the history and also perceive a deeper meaning. To show that by "creeping things" and "winged birds" he means the creatures in the sea, he added, "And God made the great sea monsters, and every living soul of the creeping things which the waters brought forth, and every winged bird." Is there a bird that has no wings? What need was there to say "every winged bird"? The word for "flying" comes from "spreading out" the hands. Hands can be "spread" too, as the prophet says: "All day long I have spread out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." This is not because hands have wings, but because "flying" means spreading out. So a creeping thing is also called a "flyer," because it creeps and spreads itself out. That is why David also says, "Creeping things and winged birds." So God made the great sea monsters, that is, the great dragons in the sea. For the other translators say, "God made the great dragons." They did not say "sea monsters" but "dragons." Among the living creatures in the sea, the dragon was the first to come into being. This is why David says, "Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps." And elsewhere: "This is the sea, great and wide; there are creeping things beyond number, small creatures with great; there the ships pass through. This is the dragon you formed to sport with." Elsewhere, wishing to show that there is not one dragon but many, he says, "You crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water." So he made the great sea monsters. "And God saw that they were all good." Why did he say "good" in the plural? Is it not because there were so many of them? But when he made the stars, the sun and the moon, many things came into being, and yet he says, "God saw that it was good." The stars are many, and their myriads are beyond counting, yet he did not say, "God saw that they were good," but "that it was good." Why? Because although there are many lights, they all come from one light and all serve the same purpose: they were appointed to give light. Here, however, there is great diversity among the creeping things, the birds and the swimming creatures. Swimming creatures are one thing, birds another, creeping things another, and within each kind there are many different ones. So he says, "God saw that they were good." The praise matches the variety of the works. "And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply and fill the waters, and let the birds multiply."

Why did he not bless the stars when he made them? Why did he not bless the plants and trees when he made them? Some things he blesses and others he does not. What is the reason for this privilege? Pay attention. As many stars as came into being at the beginning, so many remain, and nothing can be added to their number or their size. Since they were to remain unchanged in their nature, they had no need of a blessing to multiply them. But the creatures that multiply by succession and grow in no other way had to receive the blessing. I say it again so that what has been said may be fixed more firmly in your minds. For a plant, brothers, that is set carelessly on the surface of the earth's folds does not stand firm. Only a plant set deep in the earth, with every precaution, holds secure. The stars did not need a blessing, since a blessing would not have made them more numerous. But birds, swimming creatures and man needed this blessing because they continue by succession. Blessing has its place where there is no other way to multiply, where the few are multiplied and the small are given growth. Now that we know why these creatures were thought worthy of the blessing, we must turn to the other words of Scripture. "Increase," since they were small. "Multiply," since they were few. "Fill the waters," since they occupied only part of them. Another time we must ask why he thought only the fish, the birds and man worthy of the blessing and did not share it with the rest. For now, as we promised, let us keep to the sequence. "And God said: Let the earth bring forth living souls." God surrounds the earth with a twofold honor. First it bears seeds and plants, and after them the animals. This was not without reason. It was because the earth was to become the dwelling place of man. And there is more: man himself was to be nourished from it, so God honors it as the nurse and mother of this great living creature. See here too how he kept to the sequence. First he prepares the food, and then he brings in those who will enjoy it. He did the same in the case of man: first he finished the house, and then he brought in the master of the house. "Let the earth bring forth living souls." How can the lifeless earth bring forth living souls? Where did the roaring lion come from, or the running horse, the working ox, the burden-bearing donkey? Where do all the different kinds of animals come from? How did so many souls come from what has no soul? Yet the children of the heretics are not ashamed to admit that the lifeless earth produces a soul that it does not itself possess. But when they hear that God begot from his own substance, they at once set their tangled reasonings in motion and add: "Then he was cut, then he was divided, then he suffered," and all the other things they usually say. This is not the time to go through everything they say against the Only-begotten, or rather against their own salvation. God gains nothing by being praised, and he is in no way harmed by being blasphemed, unless one were to call our salvation God's gain. For he is full of every good and lacks nothing in any way. He enriches all and needs nothing from anyone. What could anyone give to the one who is the source of all good things, on whose love for mankind alone all things depend? As David says, "All things wait for you. You open your hand and fill every living thing with good pleasure." But let us bring the discourse in hand to its end, for this is both dear to us and fitting for the order of our account. The earth, obeying the command, brings forth what it does not have. Does the divine and undefiled nature not beget what it has? But again, let no one take the word "has" in too human a sense and say, "Do you see how the teacher himself has granted that the Father existed before the Son?" Rather, make allowance for the language of men who have tongues of clay and who speak to men about a nature that is divine and beyond all speech. Since we are human, we have been taught to speak as humans. The wretched heretics do not realize that they are speaking about God while putting forward arguments that are not fit to be said of God. And see their malice. When they raise their questions, they argue from human reasoning. For example, one of them says, "Everything that is begotten has a beginning of its existence." And how does he prove it? At once they say, "When you were born, did you not have a beginning? And your father, and your grandfather?" But if you answer him from those same reasonings with another argument that can undo his madness, he at once turns sophist: "We are speaking about God, and you bring human reasonings against me?" They draw the root of the evil from common reasonings, but they refuse to accept the cure for the evil from those same reasonings.

He often says, "Can someone both exist and be begotten?" Suppose I show you that Scripture says this not only of God but also of human beings. What will you do then? Scripture says that the children of blessed Abraham were begotten not as things that did not exist, but as things that existed beforehand. For Abraham begot Isaac, Isaac begot Jacob, and Jacob begot Levi, from whom came the priestly tribe. Abraham met Melchizedek, and Paul the apostle, interpreting that ancient history in a theological sense, says, "Melchizedek met Abraham and blessed him." And he immediately adds, "One might even say that Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his father Abraham." So even a mortal existed before he was born. Since the root was fully alive, the apostle counted the fruit along with the living root. But here there is no passion, no process of succession, no pregnancy, no chain of human passions. Yet the heretic refuses to say that the Son, who is, was begotten from the Father, who is, and remains eternally. "But if he was begotten," he says, "how did he always exist? For everyone who is begotten has a beginning." Among us, the name of father comes only after many stages. Take, for example, a young man who wants to marry. First he becomes a suitor, then a bridegroom, then a husband. If he has a child, he is called a father. But if no child gives him that name, he is not called a father, even if he spends ten thousand years with his wife. The same is true of the mother. First she is a virgin, then betrothed, then a bride, then a wife. She conceives and carries the fruit. But if the child is not born, she is not called a mother. Even if the root carries the fruit, she is not called a mother unless the child comes forth and gives her the title as a reward for her labors. God in his wisdom arranged this so that fathers should not boast over their children. He did not want a father to say to his child, "I gave you life. You were born because of me. Through me you were brought into being." Or if he does say this, he will at once hear, "I was born because of you, but because of me you are a father." The same goes for the mother: "You gave me my being as a son, and I gave you your being as a mother." Among us these things involve a kind of favor and exchange. In the same way, a son is not a son from the start. First he is seed, then an embryo, and only when he is born does he become a son. These things are subject to the constraints of time, they are liable to passions, and they belong to a bodily condition. But where the nature that begets is incorporeal, and the fruit that is begotten is incorporeal, how can anyone say, "There was once when he was not, and he was begotten later"? And so we say this: if God is always as he is, and never acquires anything further, then he is also always Father. And if he is always Father, he always has the Son. Therefore the Son is coeternal with the Father. We say that the Son was begotten without passion, but we do not know how to explain the manner of his begetting. True knowledge is this: to confess that we do not know what surpasses our nature. So we worship the Offspring, but we do not pry into his nature. If the one who begot were a man, he would have made the begetting human too. If he had a body, he would have begotten as a body does. But since he is free of any body, do not attach the passions of the body to the incorporeal. "But he begot from his own substance," he says. "So he begot by passion, by being cut, by flowing out." I will convince you from earthly things. The vine bears fruit, the olive bears fruit, and water too brings forth, not after our nature but each according to its own order. Every woman, once God has granted her to become a mother, swells while she is pregnant and shrinks again when she has delivered the fruit. With trees you find the opposite. Before they bear, they do not swell. When they bear, they grow thicker: the fruit grows and the root increases. The root that bears suffers no diminishing, and the fruit that is borne suffers no loss. The vine does not bear fruit the way we do. So when you hear that God has begotten, will you attach human passions to him who surpasses all human nature?

"And God said: Let the earth bring forth living souls according to their kind: four-footed creatures, creeping things and wild beasts." The four-footed creatures are livestock. The creeping things and wild beasts are the snake, the dragon and the like. The name "livestock" is used not only for the animals that are subject to man but also for beasts of burden. Every grass-eater, whether ox or sheep, is called livestock, because it is a possession of man. Scripture testifies that sheep and oxen are called livestock: "And he came to have livestock of sheep and livestock of oxen." The earth had been filled, it was rich with fruits, and it had brought forth the animals. All that remained was the master of the house. The heaven had been beautified, the earth adorned, the sea filled, and the air decked out with a multitude of birds. Everything was ready, and only man was lacking. Being last is no insult to him. It is an honor, for the house is prepared and then the master is brought in. God does nothing at the wrong time or beyond measure, but everything according to need. And see the order. First God made the herbs and the grass, and then the beasts that feed on them. If there had been nothing to feed them, the creation of the animals would have come at the wrong time, and they would have suffered from a lack of food. He made what nourishes, and only then did he prepare what is nourished. First he provides what is needed, and then he brings in those who will share in it. He did the same with the Scriptures. The Scriptures came first and proclaimed Christ in advance, and then the one to whom they bore witness came. The testimonies came first so that the one they testified to might be believed. The law came first to proclaim the Lawgiver. The prophets came first to explain the one they prophesied.

See the wisdom of God. He did not let the writings of the prophets remain in the church alone. He left them with the Jews as well, the unworthy, the fighters against God, the enemies of Christ, so that they might be refuted by them. Why did he do this, and not take the writings away from them? The reason is plain and needs no long argument: so that my preaching would be above suspicion. If I alone had the prophets, an unbeliever could object. Suppose I had dared to say that Moses, or Isaiah, or the rest of the company of the prophets spoke about Christ and about what would happen at the time of his coming. Anyone who wished could have objected: "Where is the proof that there was ever a prophet called Moses who said or proclaimed these things? You Christians may have decided to invent prophets and make up names to support your own doctrines. Must we accept a prejudgment on that basis?" But as things are, anyone who wants to object has lost every pretext, however long a plea he makes, because the testimonies we bring to support our doctrines are found among the Jews themselves. Otherwise, how could anyone fail to denounce such trickery? To keep this from being said, God allowed the books of the Scriptures to remain among them. Even if I am disbelieved because I have a stake in the matter, as though I were inventing things to favour my own doctrines, they will be believed because they are outsiders. Ask a Jew, "Is there a Christ?" I do not mean the vulgar common crowd but someone versed in reasoning and in the law. He does not say that there is none. He says that there is one, but not the one you speak of; it is someone else. So far he has not overturned the fact itself; he has only hesitated about the person. Denying a fact is one thing, and denying a person is another. Suppose someone sues me over a debt. It is one thing to say "I owe nothing" and another to say "I do not owe you, but someone else." In the second case the debt has already been admitted. So they admit that there is a Christ, but they doubt whether he is the one we preach. Having denied the one who exists, they await one who does not. Now notice how the lawgiver Moses himself brings in the Son and the knowledge of him at the very creation of man. God said, "Let there be a firmament"; he said, "Let the earth bring forth"; he said, "Let the waters bring forth." But when he came to man, Moses says: "And God said, Let us make man." I ask a Jew: if God is alone, if the Son we preach is not with him, if there is no Holy Spirit whom we worship, to whom did he say "Let us make man"? He makes heaven by a mere command, and likewise the earth and everything else. But when he creates man, he wants at last to let the knowledge of the Son's divinity peep through, as if through a window. So he says, "Let us make man," to show that the Son had been his fellow worker in the earlier works too. The Jews are hard pressed and cannot change the obvious sense of the words, so they say that he was speaking to the angels. Since they cannot openly deny what the words plainly say, they bring in their denial by another route. To whom, then, did he say "Let us make"? "To the angels," says the Jew. I ask: which are greater, angels or men? Angels, of course. Even when we reach the full measure of virtue, we do not surpass them; we only become their equals. As we are now, we stand far below their nature and are lower than the bodiless state of the angels.

Hear David's testimony on this: "What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels." So we are made lower than the angels: we are the lesser, the angels the greater. Suppose that when he made man, the lesser, he needed the angels as counsellors or fellow workers. What about when he made the greater? He made not one angel but all those countless myriads at once. Just as he made all the heavenly lights together, so he made angels and archangels together. They are so many that they pass beyond the nature of number, and Daniel cries out: "Ten thousand times ten thousand served him, and thousands of thousands stood before him." He made ten thousand myriads of angels and thousands of thousands of archangels and needed no counsellor or fellow worker. Yet to make a single man of clay he deliberates, opens a discussion, takes counsel? What is man? Is he not earth, and from the earth? Is he not mere dust and ashes? Abraham cries out, proclaiming his own lowliness: "I am earth and ashes." And what are angels? Are they not spirit? Are they not fire? Hear David cry out: "He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flaming fire." When he made the nature of fire, the spiritual and bodiless spirits, he needed no counsellor, no fellow worker, no one at all to help him with what he made. Yet when he makes the one from the earth, wretched and lowly, soon to be no more, dissolved in the grave and worn away by time, does he hold a council and deliberate? "Yes," says the Jew, "a master may, out of great kindness, say to the servants standing by: What should be done? What shall we do?" I grant even this. After such a struggle I concede that "Let us make" was said to angels. But you heard "Let us make"; did you not see "in the image and likeness"? With this argument I must sew shut the mouths of both Jews and heretics. For neither the Jew nor the heretic dares to say it. The heretic is in truth the same as a Jew, or rather worse. The Jews crucified the visible body; the heretics make war on the invisible Godhead, or rather on their own salvation. Yet the Jews too were refuted, for they attempted the impossible. For that reason they have already paid part of the penalty for their audacity: they see their own race scattered over the whole world. The full penalty will be brought upon them later, when the universal judgment is convened. The heretics too will be made to pay, at the proper time and by the same Judge, the penalty they deserve. Why, then, have I set all these words before you? Because I want to return to the thread of my argument. Neither heretic nor Jew dares to say that God and the angels have one image and likeness. For were the angels, who were themselves created, God's fellow workers? They were only ministers who sang hymns and gave thanks. They knew that they had been made, that before this they did not exist, and that they came into being by a nod of his goodness. They stood by as spectators, watching what came into being after them. They saw heaven come into being out of nothing and were astonished. They saw the sea being given its bounds and marvelled. They watched the earth being adorned and trembled. That the angels were not fellow workers but admirers, God tells Job: "When I made the stars, all the angels praised me and sang hymns."

"Let us make man." These words point to one who speaks and one who hears. See how the ray of the orthodox faith always shines: the sun, as it shines, has joined its own ray to itself. "Let us make man in our image and likeness." He preserved both the order of the hypostases and the single form of the essence. "Let us make man in the image", not "in the images", for the Father does not have one image and the Son another. "Let us make" shows the plurality of the hypostases; "in our image" expresses that they are of one essence. Who shares in this great word and this wonderful work of creation? The Jews contradict, and when they are silenced they are put to shame. The heretics rage, and the truth is attacked. Yet the teaching of true religion holds to a confession that cannot be defeated.

How, then, shall we show to whom he said "Let us make man", or who his counsellor is? For "Let us make" requires a counsellor to be present. The blessed Isaiah speaks of the only-begotten Son of God, who for our sake came to dwell among us in a form like ours: "A child is born to us, a son and young man is given." The child, who did not yet exist, was born; but the Son, who already exists, was given. "And his name is called Angel of Great Counsel." This is the child's name. He is Son because of his divinity and child because of his humanity. "Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful Counsellor." But, prophet, if you call the counsellor to whom God said "Let us make man in our image and likeness" the Angel of Great Counsel, you have not yet shown the dignity of the counsellor you proclaim. Moses too was a counsellor. He seemed to give counsel when he said: "Do not kill them, or the nations will say: Because he was not able to [?] them, he killed them." Do not stop your wonder at the word "counsellor", and do not make the name a common one. There may be many counsellors, but the unique one must not be insulted. "But you have not yet understood," the prophet says, "the dignity of the one I proclaim. Hear about the Wonderful Counsellor." For Isaiah explains what comes first by what follows: "Wonderful Counsellor," he says, "mighty God." He was right to add "mighty" to "God". Why? There have been many counsellors, and that was no reason to wound the dignity of the one Counsellor. In the same way, there have been many gods: "I said, You are gods, all of you sons of the Most High." Again, God said to Moses: "See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh." Yet the one proclaimed ought not to be insulted. And so that you would not think he is a god in the way Moses or the apostles were, he added "mighty God". Moses was a god, but not mighty; he was given strength. Being given strength is one thing and being mighty is another, just as lending grace is one thing and receiving it is another. "Mighty God." Moses was a god who was given strength. Even though he worked great wonders, he received the grace to do them. The apostles were under authority; the Saviour holds authority and gives it. "Mighty God." Not content even with this, the prophet adds "the one who holds authority", to teach both us and the heretics not to say that the ruler of all authority is himself under authority. Being under authority is one thing; holding authority is another. Do you want to learn the difference between one who has authority in his own right and one who is under authority? The apostles were under authority; the Saviour holds authority. In Macedonia Paul saw a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and kept crying out before everyone: "These men are servants of the Most High God." Paul was greatly annoyed. He turned and spoke to the spirit, not to the girl who was possessed but to the one possessing her: "I charge you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to come out of her." He calls Christ Lord in order to show that he himself is a servant. Demons obeying men was a miracle beyond human power. So that the sight would not drown out his words, and so that the servants of God would not be taken for gods, he says: "I charge you in the name of the Lord." To charge belongs to a servant; to exercise authority belongs to a master. You have seen the household servant giving a charge; now see the Master giving a command. A man possessed by a demon, deaf and mute, was brought to the Master. The Master did not say, "I charge you, mute and deaf demon," but "I command you." The charge was Paul's; the command belongs to the one who holds authority. "I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." The demon obeyed, for it recognized his authority. Let the blessed Ezekiel speak to the heretical synagogue: "As I live, says the Lord, your sister Sodom has been justified more than you." What does he mean? If you do not learn what he means, you cannot be equipped to grasp the deeper sense of the passage. The Sodomites had been condemned, for they lived in lawlessness, and that is why they were consumed by fire sent from God. Many generations after their destruction and the burning of their city, Jerusalem flourished in outward appearance but did even greater things in wickedness. So when the people of Jerusalem surpassed the wickedness of Sodom, God swore through Ezekiel: "As I live, Adonai, says the Lord, say to the faithless daughter Jerusalem: Your sister Sodom did not commit half your sins, and Sodom has been justified by you." That is, compared with you, Sodom is righteous. It is as if someone said to the heretics: "The madness of the heretics is so extreme that even the Jews are justified by it, and even the demons, for the demons call him Son while the heretics call him a creature." "Sodom has been justified by you." In passing, I ask the reason why those who did the deeds of the Sodomites did not perish as the Sodomites did. Or rather, if they doubled the sins, why were they not laid waste as the Sodomites were?

God saw not only the ungodliness of the Jews at its height but also the godliness of the believers who would come after. He knew in advance that the holy Virgin Theotokos would come forth from Judea. He foresaw the choir of the apostles, the ranks of the confessors, and the tens of thousands of Jews who would believe. When Paul went up to Jerusalem, his fellow apostles said to him: "You see, brother Paul, how many tens of thousands of Jews there are who have believed." So, foreseeing those who would believe, he spared those who had disbelieved. He spared them not for their own sake but for the sake of the fruit that would be born from them. Isaiah bears witness: "Had the Lord of hosts not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." Have we perhaps forced the text, and was Isaiah speaking about something else? Then hear Paul, the brother and interpreter of the prophets, say this: "Brothers, there is now a remnant chosen by grace, so that the remnant may be saved. And as Isaiah said: Had the Lord of hosts not left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom." For God foresaw everything. We are taught things by time, but God does not learn by experience. Again, as I have often said, he saw the ends of the ages. He saw Adam sinning, and he also foresaw the righteous who would descend from him. He saw him being driven out of paradise, but he foresaw that a kingdom had been prepared for him. And here is the wonderful thing: the kingdom came before paradise. Do you marvel that Adam was driven out of paradise? Marvel instead that the kingdom of heaven had been prepared for him before paradise existed. The Saviour says: "Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world."

Let the heretics be ashamed. The things prepared for the saints existed before the foundation of the world. Was there, then, a time when the Son was not? They confess him as only-begotten in outward form only, because they cannot erase the written word. They grant the word and steal the reality. If we say "only-begotten Son", they say at once: "It is also written: firstborn of the whole world." So according to the heretics the two titles conflict: if he is firstborn, he is not only-begotten. A firstborn is called firstborn when he has brothers, but an only-begotten is not called only-begotten if he has brothers. The only-begotten is the one who alone was begotten of someone, as Scripture also testifies when it says to Abraham: "Take your son, your only-begotten." The one called firstborn has brothers. He ranks first because he was born first, whereas the only-begotten is called only-begotten because he has no brothers. There is another point as well. The only-begotten is the one who alone was begotten of someone. It is not, as the heretics falsely claim, the one who alone came to be in a certain way. They say, "He is only-begotten because he alone came to be such." Then Elijah too would be only-begotten, because he alone came to be such, and that makes no sense. No, Scripture's custom is to call only-begotten the one who alone was begotten of someone, as the proof given above from the text has shown. Pay attention. A firstborn who has no brothers is only-begotten. But I find not one, not two, not three, but many firstborn. A strange thing! How can there be many firstborn? There ought to be only one. I have prolonged the discussion because of "firstborn" and "only-begotten", so let us resolve the difficulty. God calls firstborn the first person in his own generation to believe. He is first not in relation to all other believers but because he appeared first in his own time. For example, when the people were in Egypt, God said through Moses: "Israel is my firstborn son. I said: Send my people away to me." Here is a people called firstborn, because at that time it was the first people to have come to know God. Later, after the law and many generations, David arose. God promised to raise up the Christ from his seed, and he says: "I have found David my servant; with holy oil I have anointed him. He will call upon me: You are my Father. And I will make him firstborn." If David is firstborn, the people is also firstborn. Adam was firstborn in his own generation. Noah and Shem were firstborn. Abraham was firstborn in his own generation, and so were Moses and Isaiah, since each came forward in true religion in his own time. From these many firstborn a great church has been gathered, and it is in heaven. Paul bears witness: "You have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, Jerusalem, and to tens of thousands of angels in festal gathering, and to the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven." Christ is one of those firstborn according to the flesh, while according to his divinity he is only-begotten. Because he takes to himself those who make progress in every generation, he too is called firstborn along with them all. That is why Paul says: "Firstborn among many brothers." There is much more to say about man, but the account is reserved for the next discourse, on the sixth day, the day on which man was formed. Then, with the help of God's grace, the subject can be explained more fully, as far as we are able. We draw not on our own reasoning but on what we are taught. The spring is common to all, and all the gifts set before us are common, if only we are willing to strive with all eagerness. But let us now turn our discourse to the care of our conduct.

Yesterday we showed what the lifting up of hands should be like: hands that can lift themselves boldly because they are godly. Let the one who gives to the poor say, "the lifting up of my hands." Let the one who raises up the fallen say, "the lifting up of my hands." But let us look into the opening of the psalm, since we must certainly understand what we sing. Why do we say, "Let my prayer be directed like incense before you"? Every incense rises straight up, yet God takes no delight in the fragrance of perfumes. What, then, does "Let my prayer be directed" mean? The article is missing, so the sense is: "Let my prayer be directed like the incense before you." Which incense? There were two altars in the tabernacle. One stood outside in the court, in the open air; the other stood in the Holy Place under a roof. The inner altar was for incense alone, not for the shedding of blood. The outer altar was for sacrificed animals, offerings of bread and some other things. God commanded Moses to make the outer altar of unhewn stones and the inner one, in the tabernacle, of wrought gold. We must ask what the grace of God is hinting at through these things. It points to two peoples serving the glory of God, one uneducated and the other educated. The person who commits solecisms or barbarisms in his speech has words like unhewn stones, yet they still go to the altar. On the other hand, the wrought gold is called the precious stone. Neither is the one exalted nor the other cast out, for both there and here it is the altar of God. The perfume was made of four ingredients: stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense. The perfume is made of different things, and so is virtue. So he says, "Let my prayer be directed like incense before you", like that incense compounded from many things and completed in a single fragrance. A person comes to pray bringing fasting, almsgiving and faith. "Let this fourfold virtue," he says, "be likened to that incense rising straight up before you." Blessed David says something similar elsewhere: "Behold, what is so good or so pleasant as brothers dwelling together? It is like ointment on the head, running down [?]; like ointment on the head, running down on the beard, the beard of Aaron." He likens love to the priestly ointment, and prayer to the priestly incense.

Do you have chastity? Then you are the priest's brother. Suppose I do not have the priesthood, but I do have chastity. My chastity is the sister of your priesthood. How so? Because the one who performs the sacred rites must be pure, and I who worship must be pure too. If I have chastity, I share in the priesthood. How so? When David was fleeing from Saul, he came to Abiathar the high priest and said to him: "Give me some loaves, for I was sent off suddenly by the king and have no provisions." The high priest, who knew the law well, said: "We have no bread except holy bread, which no one may eat except the priest." He saw David's need, but he was afraid of betraying the bread of the Presence. So he asked those who were not priests for purity and said: "If the young men with you have kept themselves from women, take it." He regarded chastity as the sister of priesthood. And so that no one takes the giving of the bread to men who were not priests as grounds for blaming the priest, hear how the Saviour recalls it as something rightly done. The Jews once accused the apostles of plucking ears of grain, rubbing them in their hands and eating them. The Saviour said to them: "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry? He ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him or those with him to eat, but only for the priests." Do you see how chastity is the sister of priesthood? Do you see how God does not look at a person's rank but tests what is true?

So let us prepare ourselves for doing good and for justice, so that our fasting may take wings. A bird cannot fly unless its wings work with it, and in the same way fasting has two wings, prayer and almsgiving, and without them it cannot rise upward. Look at Cornelius, who had these wings as well as fasting. That is why a voice came to him, and he heard from heaven: “Cornelius, your prayers and your alms have gone up to God.” Imagine, beloved, that fasting is a living creature, and that its wings are almsgiving and prayer, without which it cannot rise upward. Someone like this, even without speaking, cries aloud for what is just, for virtue is a powerful advocate for righteousness. That is why he says: “Hear my righteousness, O Lord.” So prayer, almsgiving and just conduct are the first and greatest good. But what is secure and unshakable, and the root of everything, is the knowledge of God: the worship of the Only-begotten, the confession of the Holy Spirit, one faith, undivided, secure, unsplit and unparted. What I am about to say has been said before, but I will say it again all the same. In his wisdom, God allowed the heresies to take the names of their own teachings from their own founders, so that it might be plain that what they hold is not God's teaching but a human invention. So there are Macedonians from Macedonius, Arians from Arius, Eunomians from Eunomius, and likewise with the other heresies. But because he wished to keep the faith of the apostles unharmed, he did not allow its followers to be named after a man. Even if people call them Homoousians, they are not naming a man but proclaiming the faith. Paul shows that being named after men belongs not to believers but to heretics, when he rebukes the Corinthians: “I hear that there are divisions among you. For one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ another, ‘I belong to Apollos,’ another, ‘I belong to Cephas.’” Do you see that being named after men is a mark of division? Was Peter not more trustworthy than Macedonius? Yet the names of the apostles stand aside and give way to the glory of Christ. And you would cut up the faith, the undivided kingdom, the unparted glory? But enough of this. For we have the lamp and the light: “Your law is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths.” Why a lamp? Why a light? A lamp for the catechumens, a light for those being initiated.

I urge you, beloved, to keep your fast unstained: unpolluted by injustice and clean of greed. See how futile it is to busy oneself with abstaining from foods while not caring about abstaining from sins. “I do not drink wine,” someone says, “I do not take oil, I do not eat meat.” That is well and good, truly, if it is for God's sake. These things are good too. But let us look into the matter. Bread, water, wine, meat and oil are all God's creations, while greed, injustice and ungodliness are the works of the devil. Do you keep away from the works of God for the sake of fasting, and not keep away from the works of the devil for the sake of fasting? Bread, wine, oil and all the other works of God are entirely good, indeed “very good.” Paul says: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected; let us receive it with thanksgiving, for it is made holy by the word of God and prayer.” If it is blessed, then, and if it is made holy, why do we abstain? But injustice, greed and the like are works of the devil. Do you withdraw from the works of God for the sake of fasting, and not separate yourself from the works of the devil for the sake of godliness? And indeed, brothers, no judgment has been decreed against the one who does not fast, but God has threatened punishment against the one who does wrong. Do we avoid what carries no penalty and not avoid what makes us liable to judgment? Almsgiving is a good thing: to the eye it is scattered, but in truth it gathers. A farmer lends to the earth and expects the return of his seed from it. In the same way, alms seem to be given to others, but in truth they are stored up for the giver. As David says: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.” Let us fast like this, worship like this and believe like this, glorifying the Father, praising the Son in hymns and worshipping the Holy Spirit, for to him be the glory forever. Amen.
